chapters.title: File Organization
chapters.subtitle: Methods of storing data in files. Determines how records are physically arranged on storage media.

blocks.text: Types of File Organization

items: Serial
Sequential
Random
Simplest method of file organization
Data is stored as it comes
Data is ALWAYS appended (added to the end of the file)
Follows chronological order

blocks.text: Examples: Text files, transaction records, log files

items: Data is stored based on key field sequentially
Key fields have to be unique AND in order

blocks.text: HITRATE: The number of files that can be accessed at one moment.

items: Has high hitrate → Can apply batch processing
Adding new data → Re-arrange memory → Time and power-consuming process

blocks.text: Important: Sequential files have to be in order. Inserting data in the middle means moving ALL data after the insertion point by one position.
Adding new data requires re-arranging memory, which is time and power-consuming.

items: Data is stored randomly
Records are stored at an address generated by a hashing algorithm applied to the key field
HITRATE: Has a low hitrate → Few records can be accessed at a time

blocks.text: Examples: ATMs, files with usernames and passwords
Collision
A collision occurs when one data index is assigned the same memory address as another index.
Reasons for a Collision

items: A record is already written at the address given by the hashing algorithm
Two or more records are matched to the same hash address
The number of key fields is greater than the number of memory addresses

blocks.text: Closed Hashing
Move line by line to find the first available free space.
Open Hashing (Chaining)
Also known as Chaining. Create a separate linked list of all elements that are in collision.
Overflow Area
A separate memory area assigned for elements in collision.
1. Sequential Access
Move element by element to access records. Used with Serial and Sequential file organizations.
2. Direct Access
Apply a hashing algorithm to the key field. An address is generated and the system directly accesses the required record. FASTEST method to access data.
If the record is not available, linearly move from the hash address until:

items: Record is found
Empty space is found
Last address is reached

blocks.text: Used with: Sequential and Random file organizations

chapters.title: Real Numbers
chapters.subtitle: Binary representation of decimals using mantissa and exponent.

blocks.text: Overview
Real numbers can be represented in binary using a few key techniques:

items: Converting denary values to binary
Handling repeating decimals
Using two's complement for signed values
Storing values using mantissa and exponent form

blocks.text: To convert a real number to binary:

items: Convert the integer part to binary
Multiply the fractional part by 2
Record the integer part as the next binary bit
Repeat until a result comes out as exactly 1.0 — the fractional part is then 0 — or a repeating cycle is detected

blocks.text: The integer part is 7: 7 in binary = 111
The fractional part is 0.25:
Result: 7.25 = 111.01
10 in binary = 1010. Fractional part: 0.7
Therefore: 10.7 ≈ 1010.101100
The repeating section is ignored after one cycle, so the answer is shown as a recurring binary pattern.
Two's complement is used to represent signed numbers in binary, especially when handling floating-point mantissas.
Method 1: Flip & Add 1

items: Flip every bit
+ 1

blocks.text: Remember: Two's complement works both ways, so if you flip all bits and add 1 to convert to -ve, You can simply flip all bits and add one again to go back to +ve
Method 2: Place-Value Table (method used in the examples below)
Same as normal binary place values, except the leftmost (Most Significant) bit is negative.
Convert -47 to 8-bit Two's Complement
Computers cannot store decimals directly, so real numbers are stored as a mantissa and an exponent. This is the method used in floating-point representation.
Mantissa
The mantissa contains the significant digits of the number.

items: It represents the precision of the value
More digits usually means greater precision

blocks.text: Example: 5.25 and 5.2575, the second value has more precision because it contains more digits after the decimal point.
Exponent

items: It represents the range of the number
It is related to the position of the decimal point

blocks.text: Convert +47.25 (12-bit Mantissa, 5-bit Exponent)
First, convert 47.25 to binary:
This gives: 47.25 = 101111.01 in binary
Final Mantissa
Move the decimal point so it is just before the first 1:
The decimal point moves 6 places to the left, so the exponent is 6.
Final Exponent
mantissa = 0.10111101000  and  exponent = 6
Why it is needed
Floating-point numbers cannot always be stored exactly because the computer has a limited number of bits.

items: A stored value is usually slightly higher or lower than the real value
This is called rounding error

blocks.text: Examples:
Normalized form
Normalization reduces error and makes the representation more accurate. The important rule is that the first two bits of the mantissa cannot be the same:
Normalization is basically the process of adjusting the decimal point so the number is stored in the most efficient and accurate format.
Why normalization matters

items: Keeps the mantissa accurate
Avoids losing bits
Removes multiple representations of the same number
Helps represent very large and very small numbers more reliably

blocks.text: Before normalization
This starts with 00, which is not normalized.
Correct position for the decimal point
Move the decimal point to the left until the mantissa begins with 01 or 10, this is the normalized form.
Exponent example
This value is 24 in binary, so the exponent is adjusted by the number of places the decimal point moved.
Final rule

items: Move the decimal point between the first two bits of the mantissa
Adjust the exponent by the same number of places moved
If you move left, exponent increases
If you move right, exponent decreases
Denary numbers are converted to binary by splitting integer and fractional parts
Repeating decimals are stopped after one cycle
Two's complement is used for signed integer values
Mantissa and exponent store real numbers in a compact form
Normalization keeps the number accurate and avoids wasted or repeated representations

chapters.title: User Defined Data Types
chapters.subtitle: Custom data types to reduce code complexity when built-in types are insufficient.

blocks.text: A user created datatype that can be customized.

items: Good for when software does not provide a datatype
Reduces code complexity

blocks.text: Non-Composite
Non Composite: Can hold ONE value, does NOT depend on any other datatypes.

items: Built-in: STRING, CHAR, INTEGER, REAL, BOOLEAN
User Defined: Enumerated, Pointer

blocks.text: A list that is ALWAYS in order / an ordered list of elements.

TYPE Day = (Mon,Tue,Wed,Thu,Fri,Sat,Sun)

DECLARE MyDay : Day
MyDay <-- Tue
REMEMBER: values are NOT enclosed in quotes or commas here.
Pointers point to memory locations.
Let's say the pointer is at memory location 101 and is called Name:

items: OUTPUT Name → outputs Ayan
OUTPUT ^Name → outputs 101 (memory location / address)
OUTPUT Name^ → outputs Ayan (the value at that location)

blocks.text: When a pointer points toward a memory location (^Name). When a pointer points toward a value and not a memory location (Name^).
TYPE MyPointer = ^INTEGER
Makes a pointer that points to an integer.
Composite
Composite: Holds multiple values, same or different.

items: Built-in: Array, Linked List, Stack, Queue
User Defined: Record, CLASS, SET

blocks.text: Collection of different datatypes represented as one identifier.

TYPE Student
    DECLARE Surname : STRING
    DECLARE Age : INTEGER
    DECLARE Mark : REAL
ENDTYPE

DECLARE MyStudent : Student
MyStudent.Surname <-- "Esa"
MyStudent.Age <-- 15
MyStudent.Mark <-- 90.5
A collection of attributes and methods having different relationships applied to them.

items: Used in Object Oriented Programming (OOP)
We'll cover this later in Classes

blocks.text: Unordered list of elements to which we apply different mathematical operations.
ALL Elements MUST be of SAME datatype

TYPE MySet = SET OF INTEGER

DEFINE MyNumbers (1, 2, 3, 4) : MySet
MySet is declared as a set that can hold integers, and MyNumbers is defined as a MySet containing the values 1, 2, 3 and 4.
Example: A, "A"

quiz.q: Which file organization stores data exactly as it arrives, always appending to the end of the file?
quiz.exp: Serial is the simplest method: data is stored as it comes, always appended, in chronological order.

quiz.q: In sequential file organization, key fields must be…
quiz.exp: Sequential stores records by key field sequentially, so keys must be unique AND in order (e.g. 201, 205, 208).

quiz.q: What does hitrate measure?
opts: Number of files on the disk
Number of files that can be accessed at one moment
quiz.exp: Hitrate is the number of files that can be accessed at one moment. Sequential has a high hitrate; random has a low one.

quiz.q: Which file organization calculates a record's address by applying a hashing algorithm to the key field?
quiz.exp: In random file organization, records are stored at an address generated by a hashing algorithm applied to the key field.

quiz.q: When does a collision occur?
opts: When two files have the same name
When the hashing algorithm fails to run
When one data index is assigned the same memory address as another
quiz.exp: A collision happens when one data index is assigned the same memory address as another — e.g. a record is already at the hash address, two records hash to the same address, or there are more key fields than memory addresses.

quiz.q: Which collision solution creates a linked list of all colliding elements?
quiz.exp: Open hashing is also known as chaining — a separate linked list holds all elements that are in collision.

quiz.q: Which collision solution moves line by line to find the first available free space?
quiz.exp: Closed hashing moves line by line from the hash address until a free space is found.

quiz.q: What is the FASTEST method to access data?
quiz.exp: Direct access applies a hashing algorithm to the key field and jumps straight to the record's address — the fastest method.

quiz.q: Sequential access is used with which file organizations?
quiz.exp: Sequential access moves element by element and is used with Serial and Sequential organizations; direct access is used with Sequential and Random.

quiz.q: In direct access, if the record is not at the hash address, you move linearly until…
opts: The record is found, an empty space is found, or the last address is reached
quiz.exp: The linear search stops when the record is found, an empty space is found, or the last address is reached.

quiz.q: To convert a denary fraction to binary, you repeatedly…
opts: Multiply by 2 and record the integer part
Divide by 2 and record the remainder
Multiply by 10 and record the result
quiz.exp: Multiply the fractional part by 2, record the integer part as the next bit, and repeat until a result comes out as exactly 1.0 (the fractional part is then 0) or a cycle repeats.

quiz.q: What is 7.25 in binary?
10.7 in binary is approximately…
quiz.exp: 0.7 never gives exactly 1.0 — the bits repeat (…101100101100…), so the answer is shown as a recurring binary pattern.

quiz.q: Using flip & add 1, how do you negate a binary number?
quiz.exp: Two's complement negation: flip ALL bits, then add 1.

quiz.q: What is -47 in 8-bit two's complement?
quiz.exp: Using the place-value table with a negative MSB: -128 + 64 + 16 + 1 = -47 → 11010001.

quiz.q: The mantissa of a floating-point number represents its…
quiz.exp: The mantissa holds the significant digits and represents precision — more digits means greater precision.

quiz.q: The exponent of a floating-point number represents its…
quiz.exp: The exponent relates to the position of the decimal point and represents the range of the number.

quiz.q: A normalized mantissa must begin with…
quiz.exp: The first two bits of the mantissa cannot be the same: 01 and 10 are valid; 00 and 11 are not normalized.

quiz.q: If you move the binary point LEFT while normalizing, the exponent…
quiz.exp: Move left → exponent increases; move right → exponent decreases.

quiz.q: 47.25 = 101111.01 in binary. After normalization, the exponent is…
quiz.exp: The point moves 6 places left to give 0.10111101000, so the exponent is 6.
With a limited number of bits, the stored value is slightly higher or lower than the real value — a rounding error.

quiz.q: A non-composite data type can hold…
quiz.exp: Non-composite types hold ONE value and do not depend on any other datatype.

quiz.q: Which of these is a user-defined NON-composite data type?
quiz.exp: User-defined non-composite types are Enumerated and Pointer; Record, CLASS and SET are composite.

quiz.q: Which of these is a user-defined COMPOSITE data type?
quiz.exp: User-defined composite types are Record, CLASS and SET — they hold multiple values.

quiz.q: An enumerated data type is…
opts: A collection of attributes and methods
quiz.exp: Enumerated types are lists that are ALWAYS in order, e.g. TYPE Day = (Mon,Tue,Wed,Thu,Fri,Sat,Sun).

quiz.q: In pseudocode, OUTPUT ^Name gives…
quiz.exp: ^Name points toward the memory location (e.g. 101); Name^ points toward the value (e.g. Ayan).

quiz.q: In pseudocode, OUTPUT Name^ gives…
opts: The value stored at that memory location
quiz.exp: Name^ dereferences the pointer — it gives the value at the memory location.

quiz.q: A record is…
opts: A collection of different datatypes represented as one identifier
quiz.exp: A record groups different datatypes (e.g. STRING, INTEGER, REAL) under one identifier, accessed with dot notation.

quiz.q: A class is a collection of…
opts: Attributes and methods having relationships applied to them
quiz.exp: A class holds attributes and methods with different relationships, and is used in Object Oriented Programming.

quiz.q: How do you declare a set that can hold integers, called MySet?
quiz.exp: TYPE MySet = SET OF INTEGER declares MySet as a set of integers.

quiz.q: Which command defines MyNumbers as the set (1, 2, 3, 4) of type MySet?
quiz.exp: DEFINE MyNumbers (1, 2, 3, 4) : MySet defines MyNumbers as a MySet containing 1, 2, 3 and 4.
